Stated Claim / Post Context:
CIA Contractor Arrested After Allegedly Leaking Nation’s ‘Most Closely Held Secrets’ To Romantic Partner For Publication

‘he was caught allegedly betraying his oath’

Actual Article Body:
(Photo by Mark Wilson/Getty Images)

A U.S. government contractor was arrested Friday morning after he allegedly leaked classified information to a romantic partner.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) arrested District of Columbia resident Ian Brinksman, 42, for allegedly leaking national defense information to a woman he knew intended to publish classified information through her online Substack newsletter, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) stated in a Friday press release. (RELATED: Pentagon Reportedly Escalates Hunt For Leakers By Ordering Polygraph Exams)

The DOJ did not immediately respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment.

🚨 U.S. Government Contractor Arrested for Allegedly Leaking National Defense Information “National defense information is classified to protect the American people from bad actors around the world who wish to do us harm,” said @AGToddBlanche. “The details alleged in this affidavit reflect the behavior of a government contractor who exempted himself from a federal law governing the protection of classified information. The Department of Justice will continue prosecuting individuals who leak classified information and put our national security at risk.” Read more: https://t.co/uTDo8tiSjA

“The FBI arrested the subject after he was caught allegedly betraying his oath and leaking classified defense information,” FBI Director Kash Patel states in the release. “Protecting America’s secrets is a top counterintelligence priority of this FBI - and anyone caught abusing their position of trust within the government by jeopardizing national security and putting our brave warriors at risk will be met with the full weight of justice.”

Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) Director John Ratcliffe also stated that the defendant provided services to the CIA as a contractor.

“The unauthorized release of classified material poses grave risks to our national security, intelligence sources, ongoing operations, and our officers,” Ratcliffe notes. “There is absolutely zero tolerance for leaking, and anyone who violates their oath will be held accountable and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

Brinksman worked for a U.S. government agency based in the Eastern District of Virginia beginning in 2020 before he started working as a government contractor for that same agency in 2022 as a developer for systems integration with a Top Secret security clearance, according to the criminal complaint.

At the time of writing, what appears to be Brinksman’s LinkedIn profile claimed he worked for the U.S. Department of State as a foreign service officer beginning in February 2020 before working for Deloitte as a senior strategy consultant in August 2022. It also claimed he has been an intelligence officer for the U.S. Navy since March 2020.

Brinksman, in November 2025, began dating a woman investigators believe is a journalist who started a Substack account focused on “Congress, War, and political economy.” Notably, she posted “I also accept leaks,” according to the affidavit. He allegedly contributed to five of her articles from March 11 through Oct. 5 containing Top Secret other highly classified information.

Brinksman, who authorities charged under the Espionage Act, could face up to ten years in prison if convicted.

Editor’s note: This report’s headline was updated.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Nearly 1,000 arrested across France as police find potential weapons on protestors: officials

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez says nearly 1,000 people were arrested as 70,000 police officers deployed across the country amid nationwide protests.

Actual Article Body:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. Market data provided by Factset. Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions. Legal Statement. Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG.

Police in Paris, France, were captured on video Saturday firing water cannons at protesters following a march. (Credit: Lena Pontrucher/Abaca for Fox News Digital)

Nearly 1,000 people were arrested Saturday as nationwide protests resumed, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told reporters.

Earlier in the day, police officers preemptively searched protesters, and arrested people suspected of carrying potential weapons, including fireworks and ball bearings, Reuters reported.

Nuñez did not specify where the arrests were made.

In Paris, where police estimated 110,000 people marched, officers conducted more than 3,000 checks and arrested 65 people, the BBC reported.

The French Interior Ministry said about 410,000 people participated in protests nationwide, while union organizers estimated attendance at 800,000. In Paris, union organizers put turnout at 250,000, compared with the police estimate of 110,000, according to CBS News.

AMERICANS WARNED ABOUT PARIS TRAVEL AFTER VIOLENCE, LOOTING AND TEAR GAS-FILLED STREETS

Thousands of protestors march in the streets of Paris on Saturday. (Thibault Camus/AP Photo)

"Violent individuals have no place in the marches," the Paris Police Department said in a social media post. "The objective is clear: to prevent troublemakers from joining the procession, and to ensure the safety of the demonstrators."

Central Paris resembled a city under lockdown, as shopkeepers boarded up storefronts, museums closed and more than 20 metro stations suspended service.

In other cities — including Clermont-Ferrand, Grenoble, Lille and Nice — police have resorted to firing tear gas to break up unruly crowds, Reuters reported.

Also in Nice, police used a water cannon to disperse a group of demonstrators who refused to pull back. And in Marseille and Lyon, there have been clashes between police officers and hooded youths.

FRANCE’S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT

A protestor holding a French flag and a sign moves through tear gas during a protest in Lyon, France, Saturday. (Laurent Cipriani/AP Photo)

Some 70,000 police officers have been deployed across France to clamp down on agitators and prevent the kind of unrest seen during recent demonstrations, when cars were torched and the city hall building in Limoges was set on fire.

Last weekend, more than 2,700 people were arrested during protests that later turned into riots and looting sprees.

The nationwide marches were meant to reflect broader dissatisfaction with the French government, with protesters taking to the streets to air a range of different grievances.

Police officers detain protesters during a demonstration in Strasbourg, France, on Saturday. (Jean-Francois Badias/AP Photo)

The protests began weeks earlier and were led by high school and university students. They were frustrated with teacher shortages and poor conditions at schools, including overcrowded classrooms and dilapidated buildings.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The movement gained momentum when major labor unions joined the demonstrations, broadening the protests to include opposition to the government's austerity policies and concerns over wages, pensions and the overall cost of living.
